headline: High-risk workspace overlap: Roo Code can write/egress broadly while Great Expectations reads and validates shared files, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Roo Code can read/write VS Code workspace files and use MCP, while Great Expectations ingests data sources and writes validation results/documentation. A malicious or malformed file in the shared workspace could influence Great Expectations’ parsing or outputs. The pair lacks explicit provenance/isolation controls in the profiles, so the interaction is plausible.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace files without content provenance checks, prompt-injection risk is present.
IF Roo Code writes attacker-controlled text into files Great Expectations reads, Great Expectations may treat it as trusted input.
mitigations: Separate workspaces for the two agents.
Add a manual review step before Great Expectations consumes any file written by Roo Code.
Restrict Roo Code to a staging directory only.
Use file allowlists for Great Expectations inputs.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging on shared files.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Great Expectations touches validation results and documentation, while Roo Code has broad network egress and can read workspace files. If sensitive data lands in the shared workspace, Roo Code can transmit it to configured model APIs or MCP servers. The profiles show no isolation or redaction by default, so leakage is plausible in default use.
conditions: IF sensitive validation results or source data are stored in the shared workspace, Roo Code can read them.
IF Roo Code is configured with a third-party model API or MCP server, workspace contents may leave the environment.
mitigations: Keep sensitive datasets out of the shared workspace.
Disable Roo Code network access for sensitive runs.
Use a redaction pre-pass on validation outputs.
Limit Roo Code to synthetic or scrubbed files.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level data loss prevention.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Roo Code has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, and broad network egress; Great Expectations also writes validation results and documentation. Both can act on the same files, and Roo Code’s concurrency model shares state via filesystem. Without locking or coordination, concurrent edits and git mutations can overwrite each other or corrupt artifacts.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repository or workspace directory, write conflicts are possible.
IF Roo Code commits or rewrites files while Great Expectations updates validation artifacts, git state can diverge or be corrupted.
mitigations: Assign separate directories for generated artifacts.
Pause one agent while the other writes.
Require manual git review before commits.
Use branch-per-agent workflows.
requires-engineering: add file locks around shared outputs.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Great Expectations produces validation results that Roo Code can read from the workspace, and Roo Code can then act on them with shell, git, or browser tools. If Roo Code treats those outputs as authoritative without verification, a bad validation or poisoned file can cascade into incorrect code changes or external actions. The profiles show this pathway but not a built-in verification barrier.
conditions: IF Roo Code uses Great Expectations outputs as authoritative inputs, downstream actions may be गलत or unsafe.
IF validation results are stale or manipulated, Roo Code may propagate the error into code or git changes.
mitigations: Require human review of validation outputs before action.
Add checksum or timestamp checks on consumed artifacts.
Use a second validation pass for critical files.
Keep Great Expectations outputs read-only to Roo Code.
requires-engineering: add automated verification gates before actions.

E_compliance.rationale: Great Expectations touches validation results and documentation, while Roo Code handles source code and browser screenshots with broad egress. The profiles do not show a specific residency, certification, or retention mismatch, so only a limited compliance gap is evidenced. Because the pairwise compliance pathway is not documented, this remains low rather than medium.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into Roo Code’s workspace, its network egress may create a policy issue.
IF validation results contain governed data and retention rules differ between tools, compliance drift can occur.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared workspaces.
Document retention expectations for both tools.
Disable external model calls for regulated runs.
Review logs for sensitive fields.
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls.
